title: Speed & Power
summary: Fully cleared and back running. Pogos are in, broad jumps still held (none in this session). Runs as written, with single-leg calf work added back because the session had none.

exercises.name: Bootstrap Squats
exercises.cue: Heels down at the bottom; let the knees travel forward over the toes slowly. If the front of the injured ankle pinches, stop just short of it.

exercises.name: Calf Raises (double then single leg)
exercises.cue: Same primer as session 1, before pogos: 2×10 double-leg, then 2×10 single-leg on the injured side.

exercises.name: Pogo Jumps
exercises.cue: Stiff ankles, quiet even landings. If session 1 pogos felt easy and even, push height a little.

exercises.name: Wall Drill – Double Switch
exercises.cue: Drive off the ball of the foot, not the heel.

exercises.name: Box Jump
exercises.cue: Jump up, step down (don't jump down). Land soft and level on the box. Up from 3×3 last time.

exercises.name: Trap Bar Deadlift
exercises.cue: Push evenly through both feet; watch he isn't shifting weight off the injured side.

exercises.name: Half-kneeling Landmine Press
exercises.cue: Kneeling on the good side puts the injured foot in front. Fine, just don't lean hard forward over it.

exercises.name: DB Walking Lunges
exercises.cue: Most ankle-demanding lift here. Controlled steps, front knee over the middle toes, no wobble on landing. If the injured side looks shaky, drop the dumbbells or switch to reverse lunges in place.

exercises.name: Overhead Slam
exercises.cue: Feet planted and square; no rotation on the slam.

exercises.name: Single-leg DB Calf Raise
exercises.cue: This session has no other calf work, which is the most useful thing for the ankle. Slow 3-second lower, full range.

next: Pogos: 3×15 → 3×20, then forward/back and side-to-side, then single-leg.
Box jumps at 3×4 now. Next toward broad jumps: broad jump with a 2-second stuck landing, then full broad jumps.
Ready for broad jumps when pogos are easy and even, sprints pain-free, and about 25 single-leg calf raises on the injured side.
If walking lunges look solid, lateral lunges are a good next addition for side-to-side ankle control.
